newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Swiss rethink defence role for post-Cold War era.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swiss rethink defence role for post-Cold War era.

text.p: When "enemy" tanks appear out of the woods, recruits ending 13 weeks at the Swiss army's biggest training facility know just how to react.
Scouts lob smoke bombs to cover a quick withdrawal and call in Leopard tanks and mortar crews to press a counterattack.
It is a tradition that generations of Swiss men have honed as they practice defending their land from potential invaders.

But time-honoured traditions are starting to give way as Switzerland emerges from years of well-armed isolation to take a more ambitious approach to European security affairs and move towards a new role for its army which numbers 400,000.

Venturing out of their Alpine redoubt without jettisoning their traditional neutrality, the Swiss are set to join NATO's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme, which aims to foster ties among former adversaries across Europe's Cold War divide.

The move, to be launched with great fanfare later this year, underscores the cautious efforts of Swiss officials to improve their ties with the outside world without alienating a deeply-conservative majority at home.
"Switzerland does not want to stay on the sidelines," Defence Minister Adolf Ogi told foreign reporters who joined him on a tour of Swiss military facilities.

"We do not want to become a member of NATO but we want to take part in Partnership for Peace because we think it is important that we show Europe and the world that we can contribute something as a country of four different cultures, four different languages and 26 states," Ogi said.

"We have direct democracy, a federal system, and we have proved since 1848 that we can live together in peace and freedom. Therefore I think we are the most international country and Europe and I think we can give other countries something."

Berne agreed last month to join the PFP in principle. This holds special appeal because it offers an "a la carte" selection of activities that give the Swiss insight into NATO and eastern European military thinking without binding them to an alliance.

Swiss officers will observe -- but not join -- military manoeuvres and take part in peacekeeping exercises. The government remains blocked by a 1993 referendum from ever sending armed peacekeepers abroad.

Another symbol of Switzerland's push for a higher profile is the Geneva Centre for Security Policy, a peace academy that brings together military officers and diplomats from Europe and the United States to study security issues.
French Defence Minister Charles Millon and Ogi will attend the October 31 opening ceremony of the centre, which Swiss officials say will be one of their major contributions to PFP.

Swiss leaders insist the decision to join PFP marks no dilution of neutrality, long the bedrock of Swiss foreign policy. But outside observers detect signs that the political elite are questioning the value of neutrality in modern Europe.

"It is almost pathetic to go to Berne and see them, they are so upset at how they are hamstrung by neutrality," said one security expert, but he quickly added that the majority of Swiss would be appalled if this ever came out in public.
Chairing the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe has also boosted Switzerland's international image.

Every little bit helps to restore a reputation that has been tarnished by allegations that the Swiss reaped big profits by helping finance Adolf Hitler's war effort and that secretive Swiss banks stonewalled heirs seeking Holocaust victims' lost wealth.
Even as Berne crafts a more assertive role on the European stage, it still has trouble defining its army's role at home.
The militia-style armed forces, long hailed as the glue that holds together Swiss society, have shrunk by a third since the Cold War, but still can turn out 400,000 soldiers within days.
Almost all able-bodied men keep their assault weapons at home. Military spending absorbs 11 percent of the budget.
But the army remains a sensitive subject, even though the Swiss have not fought a battle since a French army under Francois I beat them in 1515 at Marignano, in what is now Italy.
Swiss voters rejected by a two-to-one margin in 1989 an attempt to abolish the army, but the fact that more than a third of voters were ready to get rid of institution shocked leaders.

The government recently commissioned an advisory panel to come up with what the armed forces' tasks should be in the 21st century and whether Switzerland still needs to draft all its fit young men. Women can volunteer for non-combat jobs.
Just why Switzerland needs such a big army remains imprecise. Ogi and other senior officials would not offer a clear answer when asked what they saw as the biggest threat.
"That's a very good question," Ogi said. "But the army is like insurance. The fact that we were not engaged in World Wars One and Two was due to the fact that we were always prepared.

"There are a lot of conflicts all over Europe, all over the world," he said, citing Bosnia, Nagorno-Karabakh and Northern Ireland. "It is very important -- and the Swiss people want -- to be ready," he added.

Even though several European countries have abandoned the draft and moved to a professional army, Ogi said Switzerland needed conscription to keep the army a cohesive force in a country split into regions with distinct languages and cultures.
"If we would give up the militia system, we would destroy a very, very important bridge between the army and Swiss society."
At Switzerland's officer training school in Lucerne, staff instructors refuse to be drawn on what current doctrine holds is the likeliest threat in post-Cold War Europe.
To be on the safe side, computer simulation of attacks assumes invaders have the most modern equipment -- that is, are bristling with U.S. or NATO hardware.
In addition to standard military tactics, officers at the school study "managing chaos" to help prepare for unconventional situations, Division Commander Alfred Roulier told reporters.
"We have studied the Los Angeles riots very carefully, for instance, and have tried to draw lessons from them," he said.

The army acknowledged this year that one unit had drilled "suppressing a demonstration by the unemployed", an unpleasant throwback to the last time troops fired shots in anger -- at a 1932 workers rally in Geneva. Thirteen died.
The government is seeking comment on legislation that would give the army a greater role in quelling internal disturbances and halting illegal immigration.
It also plans to equip it with handcuffs, batons and tear gas so it will be ready for any situation.
